headline: Bob Dylan visited the pope in a black hoodie.
summary: Bob Dylan visited Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican on Wednesday, between Italian concerts. The meeting was brief. Leo gave Dylan a rosary; Dylan gave the pope his autobiography, Chronicles: Volume One. Leo had quoted an unrecorded 1963 Dylan song against the bomb in his book warning against nuclear rearmament. Dylan, 85, wore a black hoodie, hood up.

cover_question.q: Why did the pope want to see him?

cover_answer: Leo grew up on his songs. He even quoted one in a book.
table_question: Who would you want five minutes with, and what would you bring?

5-7.script: Bob Dylan is a singer who is 85. On Wednesday he visited the pope in Rome, in a black hoodie with the hood up. They talked for a few minutes and swapped presents: the pope gave him a rosary, and Dylan gave the pope a book about his own life. Like turning up at a friend's house with a gift. That was the whole visit.
5-7.why: A visit, a hoodie, two presents. A child this age needs one picture, and the hood up next to the man in white is it.
5-7.why_long: A child this age takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script gives them the picture: an old man in a hoodie visiting a man in white, and two presents swapped. The visit to a friend's house is a frame they already own. Expect "what's a rosary?" Beads you hold while you pray, one prayer per bead.

8-12.script: Pope Leo grew up on Bob Dylan's music. In 1963 Dylan wrote a song telling an atomic bomb to go away, never recorded. The pope quoted it this year in a book against nuclear weapons. Dylan, touring Italy, asked to talk. Like finding your words in a book and going to say thanks.
8-12.why: A chain they can follow: a song, a quote, a tour, a visit. They like seeing how one thing led to the next.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out chains of cause and effect, so the script hands them one with four links: a song written in 1963, a pope who grew up on it, a book that quoted it, a tour that passed through Rome. Each link is in the article. Expect "did he sing for him?" Not this time. He played for Pope John Paul II in Bologna in 1997.

13-17.script: Dylan wrote a song against the bomb in 1963 and never recorded it. A pope quoted it this year in a book against rearming. Can a song do real work in an argument, or is it decoration? Second: Dylan was born Jewish, became a born-again Christian in 1979 and lost fans. Is an artist's faith anyone's business?
13-17.why: Two live questions: what art is for, and who owns a person's beliefs. They have views on both and want yours.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can argue about what is not in front of them, so the script asks what a song is for: a 1963 lyric nobody recorded ended up in a pope's case against nuclear weapons. Then whether a famous person's faith is public property. Expect "is he religious?" In 2022 he said he reads scripture and prays. Past that, say you don't know.

5-7.q: Why did he wear a hoodie to see the pope?
5-7.a: Nobody says. Maybe it was cold. The pope didn't mind.

8-12.q: Why did the pope want to see him?
8-12.a: He grew up on Dylan's songs and quoted one in his book.
It was private, a few minutes. Nobody has said.

13-17.q: Isn't it odd for a pope to quote a rock star?
13-17.a: Dylan won the Nobel for literature. Popes quote poets.

13-17.q: Has he met a pope before?
13-17.a: Yes. He played for John Paul II in Bologna in 1997.
